@graph.headline: Trading Edge vs Luck: How to Know If Your Profits Are Real

acceptedAnswer.text: A repeatable statistical advantage producing positive expected value per trade over a large sample, measured after all costs. A streak, an indicator, or a feeling is not an edge — an edge is the thing that survives the cost stack.

Your backtested and live trade log shows consistently positive expectancy over 100–400 trades with strict risk management — the smaller the edge, the bigger the sample needed — and your rule is written precisely enough that a computer could trade it. One log, one rule, hundreds of trades: that is the bar.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if I have a trading edge?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can place trades, but over time it guarantees net losses. The continuous drag of brokerage, STT, exchange charges, stamp duty and slippage turns a fair 50/50 game into a losing one — in India, the NSE options charge alone takes 0.03553% per side of every flip (verified 2026-10-18). Edge isn't optional flavour; it's the minimum price of admission.

mainEntity.name: Can you trade without an edge?

acceptedAnswer.text: One per family: information — the seat of a market maker who sees the order flow before it prints (almost never available to a retail trader); analytical — a chart pattern that continues 55% of the time at 1:2 risk-to-reward, backtested over hundreds of occurrences; structural — lower costs or faster execution than the traders you compete with; behavioural — the discipline to take only your highest-quality setups while everyone else overtrades.

mainEntity.name: What is an example of a trading edge?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both, on different timescales. Luck dominates any single trade and any short streak; skill — a real edge — dominates only across hundreds of trades. If the sample is small, the two cannot be told apart, and anyone who claims to tell them apart from 30 trades is selling something.
Typically 100–400, depending on how small the edge is — a smaller edge needs a bigger sample to rise above the noise. That is practitioner intuition, not a law.

mainEntity.name: How many trades do you need to prove an edge?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — they are the most dangerous outcome in trading. A win from an untested process teaches your brain that the process works, so you repeat it, size it up, and drop discipline you never actually needed. Losses at least contain information; lucky wins mislead.

It means the honest answer: your sample is too small to tell skill from luck yet. It is not a failure — it is the verdict most traders get. The only correct response is to keep tracking the same way with more trades, and not to size up until the verdict changes.
